title: Droop-FJR Does Not Imply BFJR in Temporal Voting Even Without Full Approvals
abstract: In temporal approval voting, does Droop-FJR imply base full justified representation (BFJR), particularly when no voter approves every candidate in a round? We show that this converse implication fails. An explicit counterexample with four voters, six rounds, and two candidates demonstrates that an outcome can satisfy Droop-FJR while failing BFJR, even under the assumption that no voter approves every candidate in a round. Specifically, voters 0 and 1 approve candidate 0 in complementary halves of the rounds, while voters 2 and 3 approve candidate 1 in every round. The outcome selecting candidate 1 in every round provides Droop-FJR, yet the group $\{0, 1\}$ is $(2, 1)$-BFJR-cohesive and achieves zero satisfaction. All definitions and results, culminating in `temporal_droop_fjr_not_imp_bfjr`, are formally verified in Lean.
introduction:
In temporal approval voting, an election takes place over $l$ sequential rounds with a set of $n$ voters. In each round $r$, one candidate is elected from a set of available alternatives. Each voter $i$ approves a subset of candidates $a_{i,r}$ in round $r$, and her total satisfaction from an outcome sequence $o$ is the number of rounds $r$ in which the elected candidate $o(r)$ belongs to $a_{i,r}$.

To formalize proportional representation in this dynamic setting, arXiv:2505.22513 introduced several axioms. Among these are Droop-FJR (Definition A.6 of arXiv:2505.22513) and base full justified representation (BFJR, Definition A.5 of arXiv:2505.22513), the latter being an adaptation of full justified representation from the general approval-voting framework with feasibility constraints. Proposition A.7 of arXiv:2505.22513 established that BFJR implies Droop-FJR. For the EJR analogues, Droop-EJR implies BEJR once no voter approves all candidates in some round (Proposition A.4 of arXiv:2505.22513). In Appendix A.3 (before Proposition A.7), arXiv:2505.22513 left open the question whether, possibly under some additional assumptions such as no voter approving every candidate in a round, the converse implication holds, that is, whether Droop-FJR implies BFJR.

This post presents a formalized refutation of this converse implication. We show that Droop-FJR does not imply BFJR in temporal voting, even when no voter approves every candidate in a round. The refutation is realized by a concrete election instance with four voters, six rounds, and two candidates.
result:
The main result is `temporal_droop_fjr_not_imp_bfjr`: there exists an approval profile $a$ for 4 voters over 6 rounds and 2 candidates, and an outcome sequence $o$, such that no voter approves all candidates in any round, $o$ satisfies Droop-FJR, and $o$ fails BFJR.

In Lean, `temporal_droop_fjr_not_imp_bfjr` asserts the existential quantification over approval profiles $a$ of type $\mathrm{Fin}\ 4 \to \mathrm{Fin}\ 6 \to \mathrm{Finset}\ (\mathrm{Fin}\ 2)$ and outcomes $o$ of type $\mathrm{Fin}\ 6 \to \mathrm{Fin}\ 2$, stating that $a(i, r) \ne \mathrm{Finset.univ}$ for all $i$ and $r$, that `is_temporal_droop_fjr` holds for $a$ and $o$, and that `is_temporal_bfjr` fails for $a$ and $o$.

The election instance is specified by `tfjr_ballot`:

- Voter 0 approves candidate 0 in rounds 0, 1, and 2, and approves no candidate in rounds 3, 4, and 5.
- Voter 1 approves candidate 0 in rounds 3, 4, and 5, and approves no candidate in rounds 0, 1, and 2.
- Voters 2 and 3 approve candidate 1 in every round from 0 to 5.

The outcome $o$ selects candidate 1 in every round. In this outcome, voters 2 and 3 receive satisfaction 6, while voters 0 and 1 receive satisfaction 0. The group $S = \{0, 1\}$ is $(2, 1)$-BFJR-cohesive, but every member of $S$ has satisfaction 0 from $o$, so BFJR fails. At the same time, the outcome $o$ satisfies Droop-FJR.
proof:
The proof rests on the formalized definitions of satisfaction and justified representation. By `temporal_sat`, the satisfaction of voter $i$ from outcome $o$ restricted to a subset of rounds $R$ is the number of rounds $r \in R$ with $o(r) \in a_{i,r}$. Droop-FJR (`is_temporal_droop_fjr`) requires that for every nonempty group $S$ and set of rounds $T$, there is a subset $R \subseteq T$ of size $k = \lceil (|T|+1)|S|/n \rceil - 1$ such that for every alternative outcome $o'$, some $i \in S$ has satisfaction under $o$ at least $\min_{j \in S} \text{sat}_j(o'|_R)$. Lemma `tfjr_droop_le` guarantees that $k \le |T|$ whenever $|S| \le n$. Under the embedding into constrained approval voting, `temporal_embed_sat` defines the satisfaction from a set of pairs $Y \subseteq \{0, 1\} \times \{0,\dots,5\}$. A group $S$ is $(\alpha, \beta)$-BFJR-cohesive (`is_bfjr_cohesive`) if for every feasible set $X$ of candidate-round pairs, either there is a feasible extension $X \cup Y$ with $|Y| = \alpha$ giving each $i \in S$ satisfaction at least $\beta$, or $|S|/n > \alpha / (|X| + \alpha)$. BFJR (`is_temporal_bfjr`) requires that every $(\alpha, \beta)$-BFJR-cohesive group contains a member with satisfaction at least $\beta$ from $W = \{(o(r), r) : r \in \{0,\dots,5\}\}$.

To show that `is_temporal_bfjr` fails for $a$ and $o$, consider the group $S = \{0, 1\}$ with $|S| = 2$ out of $n = 4$ voters, and parameters $\alpha = 2$ and $\beta = 1$. Under outcome $o$, both voter 0 and voter 1 have satisfaction 0, because $o$ chooses candidate 1 in every round while voters 0 and 1 only approve candidate 0. To verify that $S$ is $(2, 1)$-BFJR-cohesive via `is_bfjr_cohesive`, consider any feasible set $X$ of candidate-round pairs:

- If $|X| \ge 3$, then $\alpha / (|X| + \alpha) = 2 / (|X| + 2) \le 2/5 < 2/4 = |S|/n$, so the quota inequality is satisfied.
- If $|X| \le 2$, then $X$ selects candidates in at most two rounds. Lemma `tfjr_avoid` verifies by a finite case check over all 15 pairs of rounds that any two rounds out of six miss at least one round in $\{0, 1, 2\}$ and at least one round in $\{3, 4, 5\}$. Choosing round $r_0 \in \{0, 1, 2\}$ and round $r_1 \in \{3, 4, 5\}$ disjoint from the rounds in $X$, the set $Y = \{(0, r_0), (0, r_1)\}$ has size $|Y| = 2 = \alpha$ and $X \cup Y$ is feasible. Voter 0 approves candidate 0 in $r_0$ and voter 1 approves candidate 0 in $r_1$, giving each voter satisfaction at least 1.

Hence $S$ is $(2, 1)$-BFJR-cohesive, and since neither voter achieves satisfaction 1 under $o$, BFJR fails.

To establish `is_temporal_droop_fjr`, let $S$ be any nonempty group and $T$ any subset of rounds. Lemma `tfjr_count` checks all $15 \times 64 = 960$ pairs of a nonempty voter subset $S \subseteq \{0,1,2,3\}$ and a round subset $T \subseteq \{0,\dots,5\}$ by decision computation, showing that either $S$ contains voter 2 or 3, or $S \subseteq \{0, 1\}$ and has a member who approves no candidate in at least $k = \lceil (|T|+1)|S|/4 \rceil - 1$ rounds of $T$:

- If $2 \in S$ or $3 \in S$, that voter receives satisfaction 6 from $o$ because candidate 1 is chosen in all six rounds. For any alternative outcome $o'$ restricted to $R \subseteq T$, satisfaction is at most $|R| \le 6$, so the inequality $\text{sat}_i(o) \ge \min_{j \in S} \text{sat}_j(o'|_R)$ holds for $i \in S \cap \{2, 3\}$.
- If $S \subseteq \{0, 1\}$, some $i \in S$ approves no candidate in at least $k$ rounds of $T$. Choosing $R \subseteq T$ of size $k$ consisting of such rounds ensures that voter $i$ gets satisfaction 0 under any outcome $o'$ on $R$, so $\min_{j \in S} \text{sat}_j(o'|_R) \le 0 \le \text{sat}_i(o)$.

Finally, by `tfjr_ballot`, each voter approves at most one candidate in any round, so $a(i, r) \ne \mathrm{Finset.univ}$ holds everywhere. Combining these steps yields `temporal_droop_fjr_not_imp_bfjr`.
discussion:
The counterexample settles the open question from Appendix A.3 of arXiv:2505.22513 by establishing that Droop-FJR does not imply BFJR in temporal voting. The failure occurs with four voters, six rounds, and two candidates, even when no voter approves every candidate in a round.

This result contrasts with the behavior of the EJR analogues in temporal voting. Under Proposition A.4 of arXiv:2505.22513, Droop-EJR implies BEJR once no voter approves all candidates in some round. For full justified representation, while BFJR implies Droop-FJR (Proposition A.7 of arXiv:2505.22513), the counterexample shows that the converse fails even when no voter approves every candidate in a round. Whether Droop-FJR implies BFJR under other additional assumptions remains an open question as left in arXiv:2505.22513.

problem.title: Does Droop-FJR imply BFJR in temporal voting?
